analysis.one_liner: Triples the waiting period before ex-lawmakers can lobby Congress.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee from March 2023 until the Congress ended, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already bars former members of Congress from lobbying Congress for a cooling-off period: two years for ex-senators and one year for ex-representatives. This bill would lengthen that ban to six years for former senators and three years for former House members, and would apply to anyone leaving office after the bill became law. The goal is to slow the revolving door between Capitol Hill and K Street, where former lawmakers cash in on their contacts to influence their former colleagues.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want a government where laws are not steered by former colleagues-turned-lobbyists. A longer cooling-off period reduces the incentive for members to court future lobbying clients while in office, and makes it harder for special interests to buy instant access through newly departed lawmakers.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the post-employment lobbying ban for former senators from two years to six years after leaving office [S2][S3].
Extends the ban for former House members from one year to three years after leaving office [S2][S3].
The ban is a criminal restriction: violations are punished under section 216 of title 18, and it would apply to anyone leaving Congress on or after the date of enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Former members of Congress, who would have to wait years longer before cashing in on their Hill connections, and the lobbying firms that hire ex-lawmakers for their access. Members still in office also lose a career exit option that can pay multiples of a congressional salary.

drawbacks.text: A long ban may simply push former members to influence work that is harder to police: they can become consultants, strategists, or advisers at firms, shaping policy without technically lobbying, so the bill may change behavior more than it changes access.

For House members serving a two-year term, a three-year ban effectively means several years out of the workforce, which could discourage qualified people from running for office or push former members toward workarounds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea—making former lawmakers wait longer before lobbying their former colleagues—addresses a widely resented revolving-door practice, and lengthening the ban is a simple, enforceable change since the restriction already exists in law. The real weakness is that it may not close loopholes: former members can often do the same influencing work as strategists or board members without formally lobbying. It would still raise the cost and delay the payoff of trading a seat for a lobbying career.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Zachary Nunn (R-IA) introduced the bill on March 14, 2023 [S1][S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which was its only committee referral [S1][S5].
No further action was taken for the remainder of the 118th Congress: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote [S5].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Former members of Congress and the lobbying industry keep the current short cooling-off periods, and no restriction on the revolving door was enacted during this Congress.

for.name: Zachary Nunn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup during the two-year Congress, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's fate cannot be read as a party split: a single House Republican introduced it, no other member from either party signed on, and no vote was ever taken [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would reduce the pool of recently departed lawmakers available to lobby, cutting off the most valuable asset these firms sell: a former colleague's access and relationships with sitting members. Its defeat preserves that business model unchanged.

industries.industry: Former members of Congress (the revolving-door workforce)
industries.note: Ex-lawmakers would face waiting periods three to six times longer before monetizing their congressional contacts, delaying paychecks that in lobbying can far exceed a congressional salary. The bill's failure keeps the current short bans in place.
